title: The souq: markets and bargaining
summary: Explore the traditional covered markets of the Arab world, from Khan el-Khalili in Cairo to Muttrah Souq in Muscat, and walk their lanes of gold, spices, cloth and copper. Learn to ask بِكَمْ هٰذَا؟ (how much is this?), to bargain politely and to accept a glass of tea from a shopkeeper.

sections.title: Old covered markets

photo.alt: The long covered street of Souq al-Hamidiyya in Damascus under a high arched metal roof, crowded with shoppers.
photo.caption: Souq al-Hamidiyya in Damascus: shops on both sides under one long arched roof.

body: In the old centre of many Arab cities you will find a سُوق (market): not one big building but a maze of narrow lanes lined with small shops, often under a roof of wood, stone, metal or cloth that keeps out the sun. A small shop is a مَحَلّ, and the person behind the counter is the بَائِع (seller). Many of these أَسْوَاق (markets) are hundreds of years old and still busy every day, with local people doing their everyday shopping next to visitors looking for presents.

Some of them are famous across the region. Khan el-Khalili in Cairo grew up in the Middle Ages around an old trading inn, a khan, and today its lanes are full of lanterns, brass, perfume and souvenirs. Souq al-Hamidiyya in Damascus is a long, wide street under a high arched metal roof, with shops on both sides. In Morocco the souqs of Marrakesh and Fez wind through the old walled city, the medina, and on the coast of Oman, Muttrah Souq in Muscat stands close to the harbour.

sections.title: Lanes by trade

photo.alt: Open sacks of dried herbs and spices lined up against an orange wall in a lane of the Marrakesh medina.
photo.caption: Sacks of تَوَابِل (spices) and dried herbs in a lane of the Marrakesh medina.

body: A traditional souq is often divided by trade: shops that sell the same thing stand together in one lane or quarter. People speak of the gold market, سُوقُ الذَّهَبِ, where jewellers sit behind glass counters full of ذَهَب (gold), or the spice market, سُوقُ التَّوَابِلِ, where open sacks of تَوَابِل (spices), dried herbs and tea fill the air with their smell. Other lanes are for قُمَاش (cloth), for leather, for carpets or for perfume.

Some lanes are workshops as well as shops. A حِرَفِيّ (craftsman) may make what he sells right in front of you. In the old city of Fez, a small square is known for its coppersmiths, who hammer pots, trays and big cooking vessels out of نُحَاس (copper), and the ringing of their hammers carries down the nearby lanes. Watching how things are made is one of the pleasures of a souq, and many craftsmen are happy to explain their work to an interested visitor.

sections.title: Asking the price and bargaining

photo.alt: A souvenir shop in Muttrah Souq, Muscat, with brass pots, coloured glass lamps, silver jewellery, cloth and toy camels on display.
photo.caption: A shop in Muttrah Souq, Muscat: brass, lamps, silver and cloth to choose from.

body: In many souq shops, especially those selling crafts, carpets and souvenirs, the price is not written on the item. You ask بِكَمْ هٰذَا؟ (how much is this?) and the seller names a سِعْر (price). Then the friendly game of مُسَاوَمَة (bargaining) can begin. Not every shop bargains, though: bread, vegetables and many everyday goods usually have a set price, and some shops show their fixed prices clearly.

Bargaining works best when it is calm and polite. Smile, take your time and look at a few shops first. If the first price seems high you can say هٰذَا غَالٍ جِدًّا! (that's too expensive!) and offer a lower figure; the seller comes down a little, and you go up a little. Near the end you can ask for the آخِر سِعْر (last price). If you still do not agree, say شُكْرًا (thank you) and walk on with a smile.

One rule matters more than any phrase: only start bargaining if you really want the item, because agreeing on a price and then walking away is seen as bad manners in many places. Remember too that a few coins may matter more to a small shopkeeper than to a visitor, so the aim is a price that feels fair to both sides, not a victory.

segs: how much? (price; lit. for how many)

mistakes.why: فَانُوس (lantern) is masculine, so 'this' is هٰذَا, not the feminine هٰذِهِ.

sections.title: Tea, opening hours and malls
body: Spend a little time in a shop and the seller may say تَفَضَّلْ (please, go ahead) and offer you a glass of شَاي (tea); in Morocco it is often sweet mint tea. It is a gesture of hospitality and a way to talk without hurry. Accepting is usually welcome and does not oblige you to buy anything, but it is polite to drink a little and chat. If you are in a hurry, a warm 'no, thank you' is fine too.

Opening hours vary from country to country and even from shop to shop. Many souqs are busiest in the late afternoon and evening, and in hot places some shops close for a few hours in the early afternoon. On الْجُمُعَة (Friday) some sellers close for the midday prayer or for the whole morning and open again later, while in other places Friday is an ordinary market day. If you are looking for one particular shop, it is worth asking a local first.

Alongside the old souqs, most big Arab cities now have large air-conditioned malls; a mall is a مَرْكَز تِجَارِيّ (shopping centre). There prices are usually fixed and paid at the till, and nobody expects you to bargain. Many families use both: the mall for everyday shopping and cool air in summer, the souq for spices, gold, crafts, presents and the pleasure of walking the old lanes.

reading.title: A lantern from Muttrah
reading.ar: ذَهَبَ فَيْصَل إِلَى سُوقِ مَطْرَحَ فِي مَسْقَطَ. مَشَى فِي السُّوقِ وَرَأَى ذَهَبًا وَعِطْرًا وَقُمَاشًا. فِي مَحَلٍّ صَغِيرٍ رَأَى فَانُوسًا جَمِيلًا مِنَ النُّحَاسِ، فَسَأَلَ الْبَائِعَ: بِكَمْ هٰذَا؟ قَالَ الْبَائِعُ: بِعَشَرَةِ رِيَالَاتٍ. قَالَ فَيْصَل: هٰذَا غَالٍ جِدًّا! مَا آخِرُ سِعْرٍ؟ ضَحِكَ الْبَائِعُ وَقَدَّمَ لَهُ كُوبَ شَايٍ. فِي النِّهَايَةِ اشْتَرَى فَيْصَل الْفَانُوسَ بِثَمَانِيَةِ رِيَالَاتٍ، وَكَانَ سَعِيدًا.
reading.en: Faisal went to Muttrah Souq in Muscat. He walked through the souq and saw gold, perfume and cloth. In a small shop he saw a beautiful copper lantern, so he asked the seller: How much is this? The seller said: Ten rials. Faisal said: That's too expensive! What's your last price? The seller laughed and offered him a glass of tea. In the end Faisal bought the lantern for eight rials, and he was happy.
